title: Scaling in and out
teaches: Build a position in steps and add only to a trade that is working, size every add as a new trade from its own stop, never average down a loser, and sell partials into strength while trailing the rest, knowing what scaling out costs and what it buys.

facts.quote: In that case, you always want to buy fewer shares than you purchased in the initial breakout. That keeps you from running up your average purchase price too much.
facts.claim: When you add to a stock you already own, IBD buys fewer shares than the first breakout buy, so the average cost doesn't run up too far.

facts.quote: You can use those entries to add to your existing position or, in some cases, initiate a new one.
facts.claim: A later buy point in a winning stock can be used to add to a position you already hold.

facts.quote: Make sure the stock bounces off the moving average line and heads higher on heavy volume You want the stock to rebound and show strength, not weakness, before you buy.
facts.claim: On a pullback add, IBD waits for the stock to bounce and head higher on heavy volume before buying.

facts.quote: Never buy a stock as it's moving down.
facts.claim: IBD's rule: never buy a stock while it is falling.

facts.quote: Look for light volume on the pullback This shows professional investors are not aggressively selling shares.
facts.claim: IBD wants light volume on a pullback, a sign big investors are not selling hard.

facts.quote: Though contrary to human nature, the best way to sell a stock is while it's on the way up, still advancing and looking strong to everyone.
facts.claim: IBD sells into strength: while the stock is still rising and looks strong.

facts.quote: So after a significant advance of 20% to 25%, sell into strength.
facts.claim: IBD's own profit-taking zone is a 20% to 25% advance.

facts.quote: What about the 'averaging down' strategy of buying more shares in a stock if the price drops? My advice is, don't do it
facts.claim: O'Neil's advice on buying more of a stock after it drops: don't.

facts.quote: it is throwing good money after bad. The only averaging that makes sense is 'averaging up' in your purchasing.
facts.claim: O'Neil calls averaging down throwing good money after bad; the only averaging he accepts is averaging up.

facts.quote: The best time to sell and take your profit is when your stock is advancing and still looks strong and positive to most investors.
facts.claim: O'Neil takes profits while the stock is still rising and looks strong.

facts.quote: If you buy later when a stock is 10%, 20% or 30% extended from a sound chart base, you will be shaken out on minor 8% pullbacks in price much more frequently.
facts.claim: Buying a stock that is already extended gets you shaken out on normal pullbacks far more often.

facts.quote: Figure 2: Bad behavior - The 7 deadly sins to avoid Averaging down into losing positions
facts.claim: Hirsch lists averaging down into losing positions first among the deadly sins of managing positions.

facts.quote: Most of us have trouble admitting we were wrong and tend to buy more of a stock that has fallen, under the guise that it's cheaper
facts.claim: Buying more of a falling stock because it looks cheaper is often a way of not admitting you were wrong.

facts.quote: is to sell half on a double. This way you take your initial investment off the table and you let your winnings ride.
facts.claim: Hirsch's rule: when a stock doubles, sell half to take your original cost out and let the rest ride.

facts.quote: when they are extended in the short term you can reduce your holdings to a two-thirds or even one-third position.
facts.claim: When a holding gets extended short term, Hirsch trims it to a two-thirds or even one-third position.

facts.quote: Selling too soon can be almost as detrimental to long-term returns as money-losing trades. This is why it can be important to harvest gains and then set trailing stop losses.
facts.claim: Selling a winner too early hurts too, so harvest some gains and then trail a stop on the rest.

facts.quote: You can set profit and loss targets from a purchase price. For example, a rule could be a 2:1 or 3:1 profit/loss target.
facts.claim: One exit rule Fidelity gives as an example: a profit target two or three times the planned loss.

facts.quote: Or if your stock is moving sharply higher, consider selling a portion of your position, while letting the remainder ride to capture any further gains.
facts.claim: When a stock runs sharply higher, sell part of the position and let the rest ride.

facts.quote: when an investor can start off their trade with smaller trade sizes and only add to a trade when it's winning, they are able to start off the trade by risking a little
facts.claim: Start smaller and add only when the trade is winning, and you begin by risking a little.

facts.quote: it also reduces risk by starting with a smaller trade, only adding to the trade after it's profitable.
facts.claim: Starting small and adding only after the trade is in profit lowers the risk of the first stage.

facts.quote: Rather than closing out an entire position once a target price is reached, an investor will partially close the trade in increments, allowing the rest of the shares to ride the stock's move further into profitable territory.
facts.claim: Scaling out means closing a trade in pieces so the rest of the shares can keep riding.

facts.quote: It is also common to move your stop loss to break even or beyond when an initial profit target is hit. That way, the remaining position you have open is almost 'risk-free.'
facts.claim: Moving the stop to breakeven after the first target is common, and Investopedia itself only calls the rest almost risk-free.

facts.quote: Average up refers to the process of buying additional shares of a stock that an investor already owns, but at a higher price. This raises the average price that the investor has paid for all their shares.
facts.claim: Averaging up is buying more of a stock you own at a higher price, which raises your average cost.

facts.quote: Investors following an average-up strategy could expose themselves to increased losses if they wind up buying company shares just before they fall sharply or if the stock price hits a peak.
facts.claim: Adding to a winner raises what you lose if the stock then turns down hard.

facts.quote: Averaging down is an investment strategy where an investor buys additional shares of a stock after its price has fallen, thereby reducing the average cost per share.
facts.claim: Averaging down is buying more after the price has fallen, which lowers your average cost.

facts.quote: who bought 100 shares of a stock at $50 per share might purchase an additional 100 shares if the price of the stock reached $40 per share, thus bringing their average price (or cost basis) down to $45 per share.
facts.claim: 100 shares at $50 plus 100 at $40 gives an average cost of $45.

facts.quote: The problem with averaging down is that the average investor has very little ability to distinguish between a temporary drop in price and a warning signal that prices are about to go much lower.
facts.claim: Most people can't tell a temporary dip from the start of a much bigger drop.

facts.quote: Adding more to a position, however, increases overall risk exposure
facts.claim: Buying more of a falling stock raises your total exposure to it.

facts.quote: Pyramid trading starts with a small position, adding more when the asset performs well and shows growth potential.
facts.claim: Pyramiding adds to a position as it performs well.

facts.quote: The use of profits on existing positions as margin to increase the size of the position, typically in successively smaller increments.
facts.claim: Pyramiding uses a position's profits to grow it, usually in smaller and smaller pieces.

facts.quote: Scaling out means selling not thy whole wad at one time, but selling only a portion of your holdings each time.
facts.claim: Scaling out is selling a position in portions rather than all at once.

facts.quote: If you want to make less profit, then scale out of a trade.
facts.claim: Bulkowski's summary of his tests: scaling out makes less profit than selling the whole position at once.

facts.quote: In the first test, I bought 200 shares at 10 and sold it all at 15 (buy & hold), giving me a profit of $980 after deducting $20 for round trip
facts.claim: Bulkowski's first test: 200 shares bought at 10 and all sold at 15.

facts.quote: Scaling out half of the position (100 shares) midway to the 15 target gives a profit of $720. Scaling out is worse.
facts.claim: Selling half midway to the target made less than holding all of it to the target.

facts.quote: Price climbs from 10 to over 12.50 but does not reach 15. This time, though, your stop is at the entry price of 10 (break even), so you lose the cost of commissions
facts.claim: Bulkowski's third test: the stock rises past 12.50, then falls back to a breakeven stop at 10.

facts.quote: Scaling out, however, means you sell half your holdings at 12.50 and the rest at 10 for a gain of $220. Scaling out works better in this scenario.
facts.claim: When the stock comes back to the stop, the partial sale is what made money.

facts.quote: Swing trader Probably not. If you're too early, expecting a turn and the stock is continuing to drop, then average down if market and industry are rising and do so only once.
facts.claim: Bulkowski's answer for swing traders on averaging down: probably not, and never more than once.

facts.quote: If you want to average down a second time, sell the loser instead. Remember, you're supposed to be a pro. Admit your mistake, take the loss, and move on.
facts.claim: If you're tempted to average down again, sell the loser and move on.

facts.quote: Price has to rise after you average down.
facts.claim: Averaging down only helps if the stock turns back up.

facts.quote: I almost never average down on my trading positions. All that does is make the loss grow when you throw in the towel and sell just days before price turns higher.
facts.claim: Bulkowski almost never averages down on trades: it makes the loss bigger.

facts.quote: Others like to buy more stock as additional trading signals occur when price rises.
facts.claim: Some traders buy more as new buy signals appear while the price rises.

facts.quote: If price is higher than the previous buy or the weighted average buy price, it's called averaging up.
facts.claim: Buying more above your earlier buy or your average price is averaging up.

facts.quote: according to an article in the October 2009 issue of Active Trader magazine titled, "Scaling in as an entry technique," by Howard Bandy, the technique lowers profit.
facts.claim: Bulkowski reports Howard Bandy's finding (Active Trader, October 2009) that scaling in lowers profit.

facts.quote: Insider Tip #2: Adding to a position isn't free upside. It's a whole new setup.
facts.claim: An add is not free upside; it is a whole new setup.

facts.quote: Are you going to risk the same amount, go lighter, or go heavier? Whatever you decide, treat this as a new trade.
facts.claim: Size an add as a new trade, with its own risk decision.

facts.quote: And if your original entry point is still close, meaning you might lose some profit or take a smaller loss if you get stopped out, you will have to take that position into consideration.
facts.claim: When you add, work out what the whole position does at the stop, old shares and new.

facts.quote: Dividing your risk-per-trade by your risk-per-share tells you exactly how many shares you can hold in your position.
facts.claim: Shares equal the dollars you risk divided by the risk per share.

facts.quote: the risk of amplified losses that may occur from having a large portion of your holdings in a particular investment, asset class or market segment relative to your overall portfolio.
facts.claim: A big position in one stock amplifies the loss when it falls.

facts.quote: A stop order becomes a market order once the stop price is reached. The price you receive upon execution, though, could be markedly different than your stop price.
facts.claim: A triggered stop is a market order, and the fill can be far from the stop price.

facts.quote: Dollar-cost averaging means investing your money in equal portions, at regular intervals, regardless of the ups and downs in the market.
facts.claim: Dollar-cost averaging is equal amounts on a schedule, whatever the price does.

facts.quote: If you're more concerned about protecting your profits than you are about potentially getting stopped out, consider using a trailing stop
facts.claim: When protecting profits matters more to you than getting stopped out, Schwab suggests a trailing stop.

facts.quote: Hold your winners by selling partials into strength and trailing the rising moving averages.
facts.claim: Our rule for winners: sell partials into strength and trail the rest under the rising moving averages.

facts.quote: Trim is where to take some off: the detectors put the targets at 2R and 3R. They do not say how much to sell at each, so the course names the levels and does not invent a fraction.
facts.claim: Our trade plans mark the trims at 2R and 3R, and name no fixed amount to sell at each.

walkthroughs.title: Add only to a winner
steps: You can build a position in steps. Each new step comes only after the last one is working.
Adding to a loser is averaging down. O'Neil's advice on that was simple: don't do it.
Every add is a new trade. It gets its own stop and its own size.

walkthroughs.title: What an add does to your numbers
steps: Buy more above your first price and your average cost goes up.
IBD buys fewer shares on an add than on the first buy, so the average doesn't run up too far.
More shares also means a stop-out costs more. Check what the whole position loses at the stop before you add.

walkthroughs.title: Scaling out, and what it costs
steps: Scaling out means selling part of a winner and letting the rest ride.
Our rule: sell partials into strength and trail the rest under the rising moving averages.
It isn't free. In Bulkowski's tests, scaling out made less when the stock ran all the way.
It pays when the stock comes back before your target. You're trading some upside for a gain in hand.

questions.q: You own a stock and buy more shares at a higher price than you paid before. What's that called?
questions.why: Averaging up. You're buying more of a stock you already own, at a higher price than your earlier buy.
questions.lesson_line: Buying more of a winner at a higher price is averaging up.

wrong.Averaging down: That's buying more after the price falls below what you paid.
wrong.Dollar-cost averaging: That's investing equal amounts on a schedule, whatever the price does.
wrong.Scaling out: That's selling part of a position, not buying more.

questions.q: Pyramiding means buying more of a stock as it falls below your first buy.
questions.why: False. Pyramiding adds to a position that is working, usually in smaller and smaller pieces. Buying more as it falls is averaging down.
questions.lesson_line: You pyramid on a winner. Adding to a loser has another name: averaging down.

questions.q: Averaging down on a losing trade is the same thing as dollar-cost averaging.
questions.why: False. Dollar-cost averaging puts equal amounts in at regular intervals, whatever the price does. Averaging down buys more because the stock fell below your price.
questions.lesson_line: A schedule is a plan. Averaging down is a reaction to a loss.

questions.q: Finish O'Neil's rule.
questions.sentence: The only averaging that makes sense is averaging ___.
questions.why: Up. O'Neil's advice on averaging down was don't do it: it's throwing good money after bad. You add to stocks that are proving you right.
questions.lesson_line: O'Neil's rule: average up, never down.

questions.q: Adding to a winner at a higher price raises your average cost per share.
questions.why: True. Every share you buy above your average pulls the average up. IBD keeps adds smaller than the first buy so it doesn't run up too far.
questions.lesson_line: Adds raise your average cost. Keep them small so it stays close to your first buy.

questions.q: You sell part of a winning position at a gain and let the rest keep running. What's that called?
questions.why: Scaling out. You close the trade in pieces instead of all at once, and the rest of the shares keep riding.
questions.lesson_line: Scaling out: sell some, let the rest ride.

wrong.Stopping out: That's your stop getting hit, not a planned sale into a gain.
wrong.Averaging down: That's buying more after a drop, not selling.
wrong.Pyramiding: That's adding shares to a winner. It goes the other way.

questions.q: Finish our rule for holding winners.
questions.sentence: Hold your winners by selling partials into ___ and trailing the rising moving averages.
questions.why: Strength. You sell part while the stock is rising and looks strong, not after it rolls over. O'Neil said the same: sell while it's still advancing.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength. The rest rides on a rising stop.

questions.q: You own 300 shares at $40. You add 100 shares at $44. What's your new average cost per share?
questions.why: $41. The 100-share add is a third the size of your first buy, so your average only moves a little toward $44.
questions.lesson_line: A small add barely moves your average cost. That's why IBD keeps adds smaller than the first buy.

questions.q: Our setup trade plans mark where to take some off. Where do those trims sit?
questions.why: At 2R and 3R: two and three times what you risk to your stop, measured up from your entry. The plans name those levels, not how much to sell at each.
questions.lesson_line: Our trims sit at 2R and 3R. Know both prices before you buy.

wrong.At 20% to 25% gains: That's IBD's profit-taking zone. Our plans measure trims in R, from your own stop.
wrong.At a 10% gain: A flat percent ignores where your stop is. Our plans measure trims from your risk.
wrong.Where it feels extended: A feeling isn't a level. The plan marks the trims before you buy.

questions.q: Your full plan is 400 shares, stop $2 under entry. You start with 100 and the stop hits before you add. What do you lose?
questions.why: $200, if it fills at your stop. Only the 100-share starter was on, not the full 400. The flip side: if it runs at once, you own less of the move.
questions.lesson_line: Start small and the trade has to prove itself before your full size is on.

questions.q: Once your trade shows a profit, an add on top of it carries no real risk.
questions.why: False. An add is a whole new setup with its own risk. If the stock turns, the new shares lose, and they can eat the gain on your first shares.
questions.lesson_line: A profit on your first shares doesn't protect the new ones.

questions.story: You bought at $50 with a stop at $47. It's now $47.50 and still sliding. A friend says buy more here to lower your average.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Stick to the stop, add nothing
Hold, but lower the stop to $45
Buy more right at the stop
questions.answer: Stick to the stop, add nothing
questions.why: Stick to the stop. Buying here puts more money behind a trade that is proving you wrong. O'Neil called averaging down throwing good money after bad.
questions.lesson_line: Never add to a loser. The stop is the plan.

wrong.Buy more, it's cheaper now: Cheaper isn't better. Most of us can't tell a dip from the start of a much bigger drop.
wrong.Hold, but lower the stop to $45: That widens the loss you planned before the trade. The stop was your line.
wrong.Buy more right at the stop: If $47 hits, you're out anyway, now with more shares and a bigger loss.

questions.q: You bought 100 shares at $50. At $40 you buy 100 more. What price gets you back to break even?
questions.why: $45, your new average cost. The bar to break even came down, but now twice the shares ride on a stock that has been falling.
questions.lesson_line: Averaging down lowers the bar and raises the bet. The stock still has to turn.

questions.q: You just sold part of a winner into strength. What's the plan for the shares you kept?
choices: Let them ride on a trailing stop
Keep the original stop under them
Buy more on the next dip
Hold them with no stop at all
questions.answer: Let them ride on a trailing stop
questions.why: Let them ride on a trailing stop. The partial banks some gain, and the rest stays on for more of the move. Hirsch's version: harvest gains, then set trailing stops.
questions.lesson_line: Sell some, then trail the rest. The stop rises as the stock does.

wrong.Keep the original stop under them: On a winner, that stop sits well below. Leave it there and a reversal hands back the gain on the rest.
wrong.Buy more on the next dip: That's a new trade, and only on a real setup. It isn't the job of the shares you kept.
wrong.Hold them with no stop at all: A winner can still reverse. The rest needs a stop that rises with it.

questions.q: You bought 100 shares at $30. It doubles to $60. How many shares do you sell to get your whole cost back?
questions.why: 50 shares. At $60, half the position brings back everything you paid. Hirsch's rule: sell half on a double and let the rest ride.
questions.lesson_line: Half on a double gets your cost back. The rest rides on the gain.

questions.q: A stop moved up to your breakeven can still lose you money on the shares you kept.
questions.why: True. A stop becomes a market order when it's hit, and the fill can come well below the stop. A gap through breakeven is a loss.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven on paper isn't breakeven in a gap.

questions.q: Entry $40, stop $38. Our plans put the first trim at 2R. What price is that?
questions.why: $44. One R is your entry minus your stop. Two of those above your $40 entry is the first trim.
questions.lesson_line: Trims are measured from your own risk. Know the 2R price before you buy.

questions.q: You bought 100 at $50, stop $48. At $55 you add 100 and leave the stop at $48. What does the whole position lose at the stop?
questions.why: $900, if it fills at $48. The add from $55 rides all the way down to $48 too. Leaving the stop where it was turned a small risk into a big one.
questions.lesson_line: Before you add, check what the whole position loses at the stop, not just the new shares.

questions.story: You buy 200 shares at $10, then sell 100 at $12.50 and 100 at $15. A friend buys 200 at $10 and sells all 200 at $15.
questions.q: Leaving out commissions, who made more?

args.expr: s * (top - entry) - h * (part - entry) - h * (top - entry)

questions.why: Your friend, by $250. Your first 100 shares stopped earning at $12.50. When a stock runs all the way to the target, scaling out makes less. Bulkowski's test found the same.
questions.lesson_line: Scaling out gives up some of a big run. That's the price of a gain in hand.

wrong.You, by $250: Backwards. Selling early capped the gain on half your shares.
wrong.Same profit for both: Only if you'd sold both halves at $15. You sold one at $12.50.
wrong.Your friend, by $500: That's double the gap. Only your first 100 shares sold early, at $12.50.

questions.story: You own a winner that broke out a few weeks ago. It's pulling back toward its 50-day moving average. Today it's still falling, on rising volume.
questions.q: You want to add. When do you buy?
choices: After it bounces and turns up
Buy the dip while it's falling
Add today with a wider stop
Double up to catch the low
questions.answer: After it bounces and turns up
questions.why: After it bounces and turns up. IBD's rule: never buy a stock as it's moving down. IBD also wants light volume on a pullback, and this one is on rising volume.
questions.lesson_line: Add on strength, never into a falling stock.

wrong.Buy the dip while it's falling: That's buying weakness. Wait for the stock to show strength first.
wrong.Add today with a wider stop: A wider stop makes the add riskier, and the stock is still falling.
wrong.Double up to catch the low: Nobody can call the low. Doubling up before the turn is a guess, sized big.

questions.story: You own 100 shares from $50. It runs to $56 and pulls back. You add 100 at $55 and raise the stop on all 200 to $52.
questions.q: If the stop fills at $52, where does the whole trade end?
questions.why: A $100 loss. Your first 100 shares make money at $52, but the add from $55 loses more. With your first buy still close to the new stop, a stop-out turns the whole trade red.
questions.lesson_line: Before you add, check where the whole position ends if the new stop hits.

wrong.A $200 gain: That counts only your first 100 shares. The add loses money at $52.
wrong.A $300 loss: That counts only the add. Your first 100 shares are in profit at $52.
wrong.Break even: The two lots don't offset here. The add loses more than the first buy makes.

questions.story: You buy 200 shares at $10. It rallies to $12.50, where you sell 100. Then it falls back and your breakeven stop sells the rest at $10.
questions.q: Leaving out commissions, what did the partial do against holding all 200 to that stop?

args.expr: h * (part - entry) + h * (stop - entry) - s * (stop - entry)

questions.why: Made you $250 more. Held as one lot, all 200 shares round-trip to nothing at $10. The partial banked a gain before the stock came back.
questions.lesson_line: Partials pay when the stock comes back. That's what you buy with the upside you give up.

wrong.Made no difference: Holding all 200 made nothing. Your partial at $12.50 was real profit.
wrong.Cost you $250: Backwards. The partial is the only profit in this trade.
wrong.Made you $500 more: Only 100 shares sold at $12.50, not all 200.

questions.story: You own 200 shares from $40. It's at $50 and a new setup fires there, with its own stop at $47. You risk $300 per trade.
questions.q: What's the most the add can be?
questions.why: 100 shares. The add is a new trade, so it gets sized from its own stop: $300 of risk over the distance from $50 to $47.
questions.lesson_line: An add gets its own stop and its own size, like any new trade.

wrong.200 shares: That copies your first buy. From this stop it risks double your plan.
wrong.300 shares: That reads your risk dollars as shares. It risks three times your plan.
wrong.None, you already own it: Owning it isn't the test. A new buy point in a winner is a chance to add.

questions.story: Your swing trade is well under your entry and close to your stop. You already bought more once on the way down. You still like the company and want to buy more.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Take the loss and move on
Lower the stop, give it room
Buy more, half size this time
questions.answer: Take the loss and move on
questions.why: Take the loss. Bulkowski's line for swing traders: if you want to average down a second time, sell the loser instead. Your first add already made this position bigger than you planned.
questions.lesson_line: Admit the mistake, take the loss, move on. Liking the company doesn't change the chart.

wrong.Average down one more time: That's the second average down Bulkowski says to swap for a sale. If it keeps falling, the loss gets bigger.
wrong.Lower the stop, give it room: Moving the stop down widens the loss you planned. The stop was your line.
wrong.Buy more, half size this time: Smaller is still adding to a loser. The size doesn't fix the direction.

questions.story: You hold a full position in a leader. It has run hard for two weeks and sits far above its moving averages. Your stop is well below.
questions.q: What's your move?
choices: Sell a portion, trail the rest
Lower the stop to give it room
Sell it all, it can't go higher
questions.answer: Sell a portion, trail the rest
questions.why: Sell a portion, trail the rest. You lock in some of the run while it's strong and keep shares on for more. Hirsch cuts to a two-thirds or even one-third position when a stock is extended short term.
questions.lesson_line: When it's stretched, sell some into strength. Let the rest show how far it can go.

wrong.Add more while it's running: Buying extended is chasing. O'Neil warns those buys get shaken out on normal pullbacks.
wrong.Lower the stop to give it room: That hands back more of the gain. On a winner the stop moves up, not down.
wrong.Sell it all, it can't go higher: Nobody knows the top. Selling some into strength protects you without betting on one.

conflicts: Shape of the ladder. IBD (s1: add-ons are 'fewer shares than you purchased in the initial breakout') and IBKR (s11: 'successively smaller increments') put the biggest piece first; Investopedia (s7) starts with smaller trade sizes and adds when winning; Bulkowski (s14) says 'I do not buy half a position and then buy another half. I buy a full position' and on a fresh breakout 'I'll double my position.' docs/study/sizing_rule.md section 5 ('Progressive exposure: pilot, half, full, add only after the last step paid') is not marked as the owner's answer or quoted in his words, so it is a lead, not a house source. The file keys only what all of them agree on: add only to a trade that is working, never to a loser; size each add as a new trade; IBD's stated reason for a smaller add (it keeps the average cost down). Owner to confirm 'pilot, half, full' as his own words if he wants it asked as our rule.

Investopedia 'Scale In' (s7) contradicts itself: its definition and first example describe buying as the price falls ($20, $19.90, $19.80, $19.70 for a $19.85 average), which is scale trading or averaging down, while its Benefits section describes starting small and adding only when the trade is winning. The file cites only the Benefits lines (f19, f20) and the scale-out lines (f21, f22), and never keys a definition of 'scaling in'.

Does scaling out pay? Bulkowski (s12) and the Howard Bandy study he reports (Active Trader, September 2009) find scaling out lowers profit on trades that run; Dave Mabe, in a third-party post on IBKR Campus ('Exiting Your Trades: What Works Best?', 2025-01-31), says he doesn't scale out 'since you end up paying for the privilege with trading profit'. Schwab (s6), Fidelity / Hirsch (s4), Investopedia (s7, s8) and the owner's own rule (h01) favour selling part into strength. The file teaches it as a trade-off with both halves sourced and calculated (q19: less when the stock runs to target; q22: more when it comes back), never as more profit. The Mabe post is not cited (a third-party blog repost IBKR disclaims).

Bandy's scaling-in study (reported on s14): in a flat 2004 to 2008 market with month-long holds, averaging down ($264 a trade) beat every other test except buy-and-hold with no stops ($1,810). Bulkowski takes issue (gaps, one neutral market). The file never claims averaging down always loses; it keys O'Neil's and Hirsch's rule and the mechanics (a lower average on a bigger position in a falling stock, which still has to turn up).

Bulkowski (s13) allows a swing trader ONE average down when the market and industry are rising, and says sell instead of a second. O'Neil (s3) and Hirsch (s4) say don't average down at all. The file's scenarios key 'don't add' only where all three agree: a stock sliding toward the stop (q12) or a second average down (q24).

Breakeven stops. Investopedia (s7) says moving the stop to breakeven after the first target is common and leaves the rest 'almost risk-free'; Bandy (via s12) found a breakeven stop 'dramatically reduces profit'; FINRA (s17) says a triggered stop fills at market. The file keys only that a breakeven stop can still lose money (q16) and does not tell members whether to use one.

Investopedia 'Pyramiding' (s10) ties pyramiding to margin and leverage and calls it unsuitable for beginners; IBKR's glossary (s11) also says 'as margin'. IBD's add-on buys (s1) need no margin. The file keys only the direction (adding to a position that is working) and never says pyramiding requires margin.

Investopedia 'Average Down' (s9) says that after 100 shares at $60 and 100 at $40 the investor shows 'a 16% profit once the stock hits $60'. On the $50 average that is a 20% gain ($10 / $50); 16.7% is $10 measured on the $60 price. Not used.

Fidelity / Hirsch (s4) 'up 40%, sell 20%' example says it 'leaves you with 125% of the initial position'; the arithmetic is unclear, so it is not used. Only his 'sell half on a double' (q15) and the two-thirds / one-third trim (q25) are cited, as his rules, not ours.

The unit row's 'a third into strength': docs/study/TRADE_PLANS.md says the detectors 'do not say how much to sell at each, so the course names the levels and does not invent a fraction.' The file keys the trims at 2R and 3R (q09, q17) and 'sell a portion' (q25); a third appears only as Hirsch's two-thirds-position trim in a why.
Investopedia 'Scale Out' (terms/s/scale-out.asp) refused the plain client (403) on 2026-11-09, so it is not cited; the scale-out definition comes from the Scale In page (s7) and Bulkowski (s12).
